claim: FtsZ is a tubulin homologue whose filaments in E. coli are anchored to the membrane by FtsA.
source: The most common membrane constriction system in prokaryotes is based on the tubulin homologue FtsZ, whose filaments in E. coli are anchored to the membrane by FtsA and enable the formation of the Z-ring and divisome.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The Z-ring in vivo and in vitro is composed of a small, single-layered band of filaments parallel to the membrane.
source: In vivo and in vitro, the Z-ring is composed of a small, single-layered band of filaments parallel to the membrane, creating a continuous ring through lateral filament contacts.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by electron cryotomography data shown in Figures 1 and 4.

claim: The Z-ring creates a continuous ring through lateral filament contacts.
source: In vivo and in vitro, the Z-ring is composed of a small, single-layered band of filaments parallel to the membrane, creating a continuous ring through lateral filament contacts.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by tomography data in Figures 1 and 4.

claim: FtsZ-based membrane constriction is likely accompanied by filament sliding.
source: Visualisation of the in vitro reconstituted constrictions as well as a complete tracing of the helical paths of the filaments with a molecular model favour a mechanism of FtsZ-based membrane constriction that is likely to be accompanied by filament sliding.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by in vitro reconstitution data and modeling shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: FtsZ polymerises in a GTP-dependent manner.
source: In most bacteria and archaea, this is guided by a ring structure containing the bacterial tubulin homologue FtsZ protein (Bi and Lutkenhaus, 1991; Löwe and Amos, 1998), which polymerises in a GTP-dependent manner (Mukherjee and Lutkenhaus, 1994).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The FtsZ ring decreases in diameter during constriction through an unknown mechanism.
source: During constriction, the FtsZ ring decreases in diameter through an unknown mechanism.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a known observation but with an unknown mechanism.

claim: FtsA is a bacterial actin-like protein that forms domain-swapped, canonical actin-like protofilaments.
source: FtsA is a bacterial actin-like protein that forms domain-swapped, canonical actin-like protofilaments that are membrane associated through FtsA's C-terminal amphipathic helix (Pichoff and Lutkenhaus, 2005; Szwedziak et al., 2012; van den Ent and Löwe, 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: FtsA is membrane associated through its C-terminal amphipathic helix.
source: FtsA is a bacterial actin-like protein that forms domain-swapped, canonical actin-like protofilaments that are membrane associated through FtsA's C-terminal amphipathic helix (Pichoff and Lutkenhaus, 2005; Szwedziak et al., 2012; van den Ent and Löwe, 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: In C. crescentus cells, FtsZ filaments form a continuous ring at division sites.
source: Careful analysis of cellular tomograms (Video 1 and Figure 1A, bottom) revealed that the dots were in fact 2D projections of filamentous structures encircling the cell and likely forming a continuous ring, disrupted in the images at the top and bottom by the missing wedge of the tomography method.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by tomography data shown in Figure 1A and Video 1.

claim: FtsZ filaments in C. crescentus are located 15 ± 2 nm from the inner membrane.
source: The filaments were at a distance of 15 ± 2 nm from the inner membrane (Figure 1B), as previously reported (Li et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1B and a previous study.

claim: Continuous FtsZ rings were detected in 20 out of 28 dividing C. crescentus cells after tomography.
source: We could detect the filamentous rings in 20 out of 28 dividing cells after tomography.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a quantitative observation.

claim: In E. coli B/r H266 cells, FtsZ filaments are located 16 nm from the inner membrane.
source: Although the E. coli cells were thicker than C. crescentus, we found the wild-type filaments still discernible, most obviously when imaged along the long axis of cells (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2, especially B and D; Video 2), and these were 16 nm away from the IM.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1C and supplementary figures.

claim: E. coli Z-rings are continuous and consist of single-layered bands that are 5–10 filaments wide.
source: Based on these observations we concluded that E. coli Z-rings were, like in C. crescentus, probably continuous and consisted of single-layered bands that are 5–10 filaments wide.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from tomography observations.

claim: FtsZ(D212A) is a mutant protein that hydrolyses GTP much more slowly than wild-type FtsZ.
source: In order to investigate if the filaments imaged in wild-type cells so far contained FtsZ protein, we over-expressed FtsZ(D212A), a mutant protein that hydrolyses GTP much more slowly (Redick et al., 2005) in E. coli B/r H266 cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Over-expression of FtsZ(D212A) to 2.5-fold total FtsZ forms a wide single layer of filaments at the division site.
source: When over-expressed to 2.5-fold total FtsZ (Figure 1D), the protein formed a wide single layer of filaments at the division site (Figure 1E, see also Video 3 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3), very similar to the bands seen in unmodified cells, but wider and containing more filaments as would be expected because there is now more FtsZ protein in the cell and filament dynamics have been reduced because of the GTPase-reducing mutation D212A.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figures 1D and 1E.

claim: The FtsZ filament band most likely consists of doublets of individual protofilaments.
source: The band of filaments most likely consisted of doublets of individual protofilaments, as is indicated in Figure 1G, which shows a cell with higher expression level (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1G.

claim: Filaments within doublets are on average 6.8 nm apart.
source: The filaments were on average 6.8 nm apart (n = 17, distance between centres of adjacent filaments within a doublet, Figure 1G, lower).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1G.

claim: Extending the C-terminal linker of FtsZ increases the distance between the FtsZ ring and the inner membrane from 16 nm to 16–21 nm.
source: (a) Introducing extra amino acids into the flexible linker (Buske and Levin, 2013; Gardner et al., 2013) within FtsZ that separates the globular N-terminal domain of FtsZ from the small C-terminal helix that binds FtsZ's membrane anchor, FtsA (Ma and Margolin, 1999; Szwedziak et al., 2012), increased the distance between the FtsZ ring and the IM from 16 nm to a somewhat variable 16–21 nm (Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1H and supplementary figures.

claim: Replacing the C-terminal FtsA-interacting helix with a membrane-targeting sequence from MinD shortens the distance from the inner membrane to 10 nm.
source: (b) Removing the C-terminal FtsA-interacting helix and replacing it with a membrane-targeting sequence (mts) from MinD protein (Hu and Lutkenhaus, 2003) shortened the distance from the IM to 10 nm.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: FtsZ with a membrane-targeting sequence replacing the FtsA-interacting helix does not produce cell constrictions.
source: No constrictions of the cells were observed (Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1I.

claim: Removing the C-terminal FtsA-interacting helix from FtsZ detaches the filaments from the membrane.
source: (c) Removing the C-terminal FtsA-interacting helix from FtsZ detached the filaments from the membrane, making them appear throughout the cytoplasm (Figure 1J and Figure 1—figure supplement 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1J.

claim: Removing most amino acids between the C-terminal FtsA-interacting helix and the globular body of FtsZ causes a minicell phenotype.
source: (d) Finally, removing most amino acids between the C-terminal FtsA-interacting helix and the globular body of FtsZ caused a minicell phenotype.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: The longitudinal subunit repeat of FtsZ filaments is around 4 nm.
source: Because of their size, minicells produce tomograms of higher quality and it was possible to determine the longitudinal subunit repeat of the filaments to be around 4 nm, very close to the expected value of 4.2 nm for FtsZ (Figure 1K and L and Figure 1—figure supplement 4G) (Erickson et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1K and L and a citation.

claim: Simultaneous over-expression of FtsZ and FtsA leads to additional division sites in E. coli.
source: Encouraged by reports that simultaneous over-expression of FtsZ and its membrane anchor FtsA led to additional division sites (Begg et al., 1998), we imaged E. coli cells in which extra FtsZ(D212A) and FtsA were produced from a bicistronic expression vector, by electron cryotomography (Figure 2A–E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Over-expression of FtsZ(D212A) and FtsA (twofold to fourfold total vs WT) produces a severe phenotype with many extra constrictions.
source: Providing just these two proteins in excess (twofold to fourfold total vs WT) produced a severe phenotype with many extra constrictions visible (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 2A and B.

claim: When the FtsZ to FtsA ratio is altered to be close to 1:1, FtsA filaments become visible at constricting division sites.
source: Since in these cells the normal FtsZ to FtsA ratio had been altered to be close to 1:1, from normally 5 FtsZ:1 FtsA (Rueda et al., 2003), FtsA filaments became visible at the constricting division sites (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 2C-E and a citation.

claim: FtsA is located between the inner membrane and FtsZ, being 8 nm away from both.
source: In this way, an artificially strong 'FtsA ring' became apparent, indicating that FtsA is located between the IM and FtsZ, being 8 nm away from both (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 2D and E.

claim: FtsZ(D212A) and FtsA-over-expressing E. coli cells divide and separate, showing a strong minicell phenotype.
source: We then demonstrated that the FtsZ(D212A) and FtsA-over-expressing E. coli cells, we had imaged at high-resolution with electron cryotomography, were dividing and separating, despite looking quite distorted. For this, we employed structured illumination microscopy (SIM) on live cells (Figure 2F). The cells showed a strong minicell phenotype, while performing many cell divisions randomly distributed along the cell length.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 2F.

claim: The extra constrictions and division sites produced by FtsZ and FtsA over-expression are functional and lead to complete cell separation.
source: This indicated to us that the extra constrictions and division sites were functional in the sense that they led to complete cell separation (abscission).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the SIM data.

claim: FtsZ and FtsA may be central components of the inner membrane constriction force generator.
source: We concluded that the ability to produce extra constriction sites and divisions by just providing more FtsZ and FtsA indicates that these two proteins may be central components of the IM constriction force generator that is localised within the inner division apparatus (Rico et al., 2013) and that it may be possible to reconstitute membrane constriction with just the two of them.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the over-expression experiments.

claim: TmFtsZ and TmFtsA form spirals on a flat lipid monolayer.
source: When added onto a flat lipid monolayer, TmFtsZ and TmFtsA formed striking spirals (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: Filaments forming spirals on lipid monolayers tend to form weak doublets.
source: The filaments forming the spirals tended to form weak doublets and in the centre of the spirals, white material was visible that may have been lipid that had been pushed up by the spiral constricting, possibly via a sliding filament mechanism as has previously been observed for FtsZ alone by AFM (Mingorance et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 3A and a citation.

claim: When TmFtsA and TmFtsZ are encapsulated in liposomes, constriction sites are efficiently formed.
source: Constriction sites are efficiently formed when TmFtsA and TmFtsZ are encapsulated in liposomes that have sizes comparable to bacterial cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 3 legend with reference to panels C-G.

claim: Constriction sites are only formed where a ring made of TmFtsA and TmFtsZ is present.
source: Importantly, constriction sites are only formed where a ring made of the two proteins is present (black arrowheads) and not at other sites where filaments are located.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 3 legend.

claim: The distance between TmFtsZ and the membrane in liposomes is 12 nm.
source: The distance of 12 nm between TmFtsZ and the membrane (inset J) resembles that found in over-expressing cells (see Figure 2G and also Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 3 legend with reference to inset J.

claim: Liposomes are constricted (partially) in the absence of added nucleotide.
source: (E) Intriguingly, liposomes are being constricted (partially) in the absence of added nucleotide.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 3 legend with reference to panel E.

claim: When both TmFtsZ and TmFtsA are included on the inside of liposomes, clear constriction sites appear.
source: Amazingly, when both TmFtsZ and TmFtsA were included on the inside of liposomes, clear constriction sites appeared and these occurred only when supported by filaments (Figure 3C–G).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 3C-G.

claim: Constrictions only appear where there are rings of filaments in liposomes.
source: It is very important to note that constrictions only appeared where there were rings of filaments.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an important observation.

claim: Constriction is largely nucleotide hydrolysis independent.
source: Constriction itself, however, was largely nucleotide hydrolysis independent since not adding any nucleotide produced constrictions as well, and they appeared even tighter (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 3E.

claim: The TmFtsAZ rings in liposomes were between 30 and 90 nm in diameter.
source: The TmFtsAZ rings were between 30 and 90 nm in diameter, when we looked at several different liposomes, and the filaments were on average 7.8 nm apart (n = 16) laterally (Figure 4B,C) as compared to 6.8 nm seen in E. coli cells (within doublets).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 4B and C.

claim: Filaments in TmFtsAZ rings are on average 7.8 nm apart laterally.
source: The TmFtsAZ rings were between 30 and 90 nm in diameter, when we looked at several different liposomes, and the filaments were on average 7.8 nm apart (n = 16) laterally (Figure 4B,C) as compared to 6.8 nm seen in E. coli cells (within doublets).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 4B and C.

claim: The rings of filaments in liposomes are always closed and continuous without gaps.
source: The rings were always closed, continuous without gaps, with some possibly consisting of one double filament forming a helix (Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Video 6) and others containing several shorter filaments in a helix-like arrangement (Figure 4A stereo view and Video 10).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 4A and supplementary figures.

claim: Filaments in liposome constrictions are arranged close to 90° with respect to the liposome membrane tangent.
source: When the filaments were investigated end-on, they appeared to always be arranged close to 90° with respect to the liposome membrane tangent (Figure 4C), which was also observed for the filaments in cells (Figure 2C,G).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 4C.

claim: Constriction requires the filaments to slide along each other as the ring decreases in diameter.
source: Given a continuous ring, at least in the in vitro situation, with no GTP turnover (or no added nucleotide) there is no filament shortening, meaning constriction requires the filaments to slide along each other as the ring decreases in diameter and the membrane deforms.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an inference from the continuous ring observation.

claim: Force generation is dependent on a closed ring, making the system self-regulating.
source: Since in this model force generation is dependent on a closed ring, the system becomes self-regulating since constriction will only commence after a complete ring has formed.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an inference from the model.

claim: If the cell is too large or not enough FtsZ is available, constriction will not begin.
source: If the cell is too large or not enough FtsZ is available, constriction will not begin.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a consequence of the self-regulating mechanism.

claim: Maximising filament overlap via sliding may drive constriction of closed rings.
source: A. When the overlap between the filaments that are attracted to each other increases, more and more binding energy is produced. This has been proposed before to be theoretically sufficient for the constriction process (Lan et al., 2009) (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a proposed mechanism with a supporting citation.

claim: The repeat length mismatch of FtsA and FtsZ may provide a driver of constriction.
source: B. The second possible driver of constriction comes from the repeat length mismatch of FtsA and FtsZ (Szwedziak et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a proposed mechanism with a supporting citation.

claim: GTP hydrolysis by FtsZ may be required for filament shortening to overcome kinetic barriers during constriction.
source: C. Why does FtsZ hydrolyse GTP then? We speculate that when constriction starts at large diameters (1 µm in E. coli), longer GTP-induced FtsZ filaments are needed to reach reliably around the cell in order to produce overlap for the ring and 'force engagement' to start the process. However, increasing overlap, developing as the constriction progresses, might lead to a kinetic barrier of sliding through avidity and the filaments would then have to be shortened. Formally this provides a third possible driver of constriction, at least for large constriction distances.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as speculation about the role of GTP hydrolysis.

claim: Nucleotide binding/hydrolysis is required solely for filament growth/shrinkage to maintain the dynamic state of the FtsZ ring in cells.
source: We suggest that nucleotide binding/hydrolysis is required solely for filament growth/shrinkage as these are essential to maintain the dynamic state of the FtsZ ring in cells.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a suggested interpretation of the data.

claim: In vitro liposome constrictions and in vivo cell division may utilise a different set of energetic drivers.
source: Taken together, we envisage that in vitro liposome constrictions and in vivo cell division quite possibly utilise a different set of energetic drivers (a–c); for example, GTP hydrolysis was not required in vitro but clearly plays a role in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the data.

claim: Cell wall synthesis in the periplasm, guided by the Z-ring through the divisome, likely provides additional force in cells.
source: And of course, it is likely that the cell wall synthesis in the periplasm, guided by the Z-ring through the divisome, provides additional force in cells.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a speculation about additional forces in vivo.

claim: FtsZ-based cell division is not functioning in artificial L-forms.
source: So far, wall-less bacterial L-forms have not shed light on this interdependence of cell wall synthesis and the FtsZ ring since artificial L-forms were found to divide by blebbing, most likely a mechanism that is not actively supported by cellular machinery (Leaver et al., 2009). FtsZ-based cell division is not functioning in these L-forms and we suggest this may be because L-forms are too large for Z-rings to close, given the amounts of FtsAZ present.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation and speculation.

claim: The change from a flat band of filaments towards helical spirals enables inward force to be developed on each side of the constriction.
source: Figure 5D, middle shows how an intermediate between the rings and the domes (as is present in the liposome constriction shown in Figure 4A, bottom right and Video 9) may explain abscission, since the protein ring would normally be in the way of membrane fusion/fission at the end. The change from a flat band of filaments towards the helical spirals enables inward force to be developed on each side of the constriction, with a helical spiral on each side.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with reference to Figure 5D and Figure 4A.

claim: Membrane constriction with ESCRT-III and dynamin filaments has been suggested to involve sliding helical filaments.
source: It is important to mention that membrane constriction with ESCRT-III and dynamin filaments has also been suggested to involve sliding helical filaments (Roux et al., 2006; Guizetti et al., 2011) and similar arrangements to those depicted in Figure 5D, right were predicted for the ESCRT-III system (Fabrikant et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: FtsZ is a bacterial tubulin homologue.
source: In most bacteria and archaea, this is guided by a ring structure containing the bacterial tubulin homologue FtsZ protein (Bi and Lutkenhaus, 1991; Löwe and Amos, 1998)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The C-terminal tail of FtsZ links it to other components of the divisome.
source: The C-terminal tail of FtsZ links it to other components of the divisome, an ensemble of many proteins that facilitates essential functions during the cell division process, most importantly remodelling of the cell envelope.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction.

claim: In E. coli, binding of the FtsZ tail to ZipA and FtsA anchors the FtsZ ring to the membrane.
source: In Escherichia coli, binding of the FtsZ tail to ZipA and possibly more importantly to FtsA anchor the FtsZ ring to the membrane (Pichoff and Lutkenhaus, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: SulA is induced during the SOS stress response and sequesters FtsZ monomers, stopping FtsZ polymerisation.
source: For example, SulA is induced during the SOS stress response and sequesters monomers, stopping FtsZ polymerisation (Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Previous tomography data have been interpreted to show scattered individual FtsZ filaments some distance away from the membrane.
source: Equally, tomography data have been interpreted to show scattered individual FtsZ filaments, some precise distance away from the membrane (Li et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Reconstitution experiments with FtsZ and FtsA showed dynamic behaviour and liposome constrictions.
source: Reconstitution experiments with FtsZ and FtsA showed dynamic behaviour and liposome constrictions (Osawa and Erickson, 2013; Loose and Mitchison, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The missing wedge problem in electron tomography is caused by the inability to tilt the specimen much beyond 65°.
source: The long-standing problem of the missing wedge in electron tomography caused by our current inability to tilt the specimen much beyond 65° (Figure 1A, bottom, white triangle, see also Figure 1—figure supplement 1 for more details on the missing wedge problem related to this study)
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1A and supplementary figures.

claim: The protein filaments at division sites are visible and uninterrupted everywhere the missing wedge allows.
source: It is important to note, however, that the protein filaments are visible and uninterrupted everywhere the missing wedge allows it, as can be gauged from the disappearance of the cell membrane and envelope (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1A and B.

claim: The normal FtsZ to FtsA ratio in E. coli is 5:1.
source: Since in these cells the normal FtsZ to FtsA ratio had been altered to be close to 1:1, from normally 5 FtsZ:1 FtsA (Rueda et al., 2003)
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: TmFtsZ and TmFtsA over-expression in E. coli produces minicells.
source: Just to confirm that TmFtsZ and TmFtsA formed structures similar to the E. coli counterparts in vivo, we over-expressed TmFtsZ and TmFtsA in E. coli and imaged the sample by electron cryotomography (Figure 2G). Minicells were formed
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 2G.

claim: The distance of TmFtsZ to the inner membrane in E. coli is 12 nm.
source: The distance of TmFtsZ to the IM was shorter at 12 nm; this was expected because the linker between the very C-terminal TmFtsA-interacting helix and the body of TmFtsZ is much shorter, measuring around nine amino acids.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: TmFtsA binds to the inside of the liposome membrane via its amphipathic helix.
source: The architecture is easily explained with TmFtsA-binding to the inside of the liposome membrane via its amphipathic helix, presumably polymerising, and FtsZ polymerising on top of FtsA, binding to it via its C-terminal FtsA-binding peptide (Pichoff and Lutkenhaus, 2005; Szwedziak et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: GTP addition produces the most bilobed liposomes in the reconstitution experiments.
source: Nucleotide presence had some influence on the appearance of these constricted liposomes as GTP addition produced the most bilobed liposomes.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: Significant hydrolysis of GTP to GDP is not expected for TmFtsZ because it is a hyperthermophilic protein.
source: Given that TmFtsZ is a hyperthermophilic protein, significant hydrolysis of GTP to GDP is not expected.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the protein's origin.

claim: The rings in liposomes were always perfectly round, in contrast to the rest of the liposomes.
source: That opposing forces from the filaments and the membrane surface are at work is most evident from the fact that the rings were always perfectly round, in contrast to the rest of the liposomes (Figure 4B, middle, Video 10).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with reference to Figure 4B and Video 10.

claim: The lateral spacing between FtsZ filaments in C. crescentus cells was previously found to be 9.3 nm.
source: In C. crescentus cells, the lateral spacing between filaments was found to be 9.3 nm previously (Li et al., 2007)(Li et al., 2007)
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: AFM using only FtsZ observed spiral condensation with a lateral distance of 12 nm.
source: AFM using only FtsZ, but observing spiral condensation, provided an even larger distance of 12 nm (Mingorance et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: The filaments in the FtsZ ring interact transiently and direct contact is localised to only a few small regions within the ring at a time.
source: One may conclude that the filaments in the FtsZ ring interact transiently and direct contact is localised to only a few small regions within the ring at a time.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the measurements.

claim: FtsZ(D212G) mutant generates prominent constrictions of tubular liposomes in vitro.
source: However, it has been reported that the GTP hydrolysis-deficient FtsZ(D212G) mutant generates prominent constrictions of tubular liposomes in vitro (Osawa and Erickson, 2011)
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: FtsZ(D212G) functions in cell division in E. coli.
source: and functions in cell division in E. coli (Bi and Lutkenhaus, 1992; Trusca et al., 1998; Osawa and Erickson, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The use of non-hydrolysable GTP analogues did not impair the formation of condensed FtsZ structures on mica.
source: Furthermore, the use of non-hydrolysable GTP analogues did not impair the formation of condensed FtsZ structures on mica (Hörger et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: FtsZ ring dynamics are maintained by continual depolymerisation and re-polymerisation through nucleotide turnover.
source: Continual depolymerisation and re-polymerisation through nucleotide turnover by FtsZ and/or FtsA, as shown in vivo by FRAP (Stricker et al., 2002)
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: FtsZ may leave the septum earlier than previously thought.
source: It remains to be seen if FtsZ is involved in final abscission since it has recently been reported that FtsZ might leave the septum earlier (Söderström et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Liposomes used in the reconstitution experiments were around 300 nm in diameter.
source: The liposomes were around 300 nm in diameter, similar to that of a small bacterial cell.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: The protein filaments in liposomes were arranged into three distinct structures: arcs, spirals, and rings.
source: The protein filaments were arranged into three distinct structures: arcs that were mostly single filaments, presumably formed by the co-polymerisation of TmFtsZ and TmFtsA, showing the characteristic curvature caused by the repeat mismatch (Szwedziak et al., 2012); spirals with decreasing curvature that appeared in perfectly spherical areas of the liposomes; and rings of filaments, appearing as bands in projection, formed around liposome constriction sites, with varying diameters.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Co-polymerisation of FtsZ and FtsA leads to bending and curvature because the subunit repeat lengths are roughly 4 and 5 nm, respectively.
source: As was suggested previously, the co-polymerisation of FtsZ and FtsA will lead to bending and curvature because the subunit repeat lengths of FtsZ and FtsA are roughly 4 and 5 nm, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A) (Szwedziak et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Most liposomes were initially perfectly spherical and deformed over a 30-min period after detergent dilution.
source: We demonstrated with a time-lapse experiment that liposomes did not form around pre-existing FtsZ scaffolds since we observed that most liposomes were initially perfectly spherical and that they deformed over a 30-min period, after which most of them were heavily misshapen (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C,E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: The Caulobacter crescentus tomogram has been deposited in the EM databank with accession number EMD-2814.
source: The Caulobacter crescentus tomogram shown in Figure 1A has been deposited in the EM databank with accession number EMD-2814.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The edited tomogram of TmFtsAZ constricting a liposome has been deposited with accession number EMD-2815.
source: The edited tomogram of TmFtsAZ constricting a liposome, as shown in Figures 4A and 5A and Video 10, has been deposited with accession number EMD-2815.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.
